explanation: These are the four Cratchit children whose first names Dickens gives. The family also has two younger children who are not named.
The Cratchits share goose and pudding, Scrooge eats gruel alone, and his gift of a turkey expresses his new generosity.
Burning coal fuels the fires. Candles and the second spirit’s torch also provide flames. These sources of warmth and light recur throughout the story.
A waistcoat, neckcloth, bedtime hat, scarf and decorative strip of fabric are all worn on the body. Bed curtains are furnishings, not clothing.
These are given names of male characters. Scrooge, Marley and Cratchit are surnames. Tiny is a description added to Tim’s name.
These techniques use comparison, nonliteral description, human qualities or exaggeration. Alliteration concerns repeated sounds instead.
These name grammatical classes: naming words, actions or states, descriptions of nouns, and words that modify verbs or other expressions.

group: Named places in the London setting
explanation: London is the city. The Cratchits live in Camden Town, Bob slides on Cornhill, and the Royal Exchange belongs to the city’s world of business.
Marley’s chain contains steel versions of objects associated with money, business and security. His old priorities have become his burden.
Fan visits him at school, Belle ends their engagement, and Fezziwig and Dick Wilkins appear during his apprenticeship in Stave Two.
These describe a learner in a trade, an office worker, a cleaner, a laundry worker, a hat seller, a poultry trader and someone who arranges funerals.
These five participles appear together before the description of Scrooge as a covetous old sinner. Their forceful movements make his greed seem active and aggressive.

group: Being alone or cut off from others
explanation: These suggest separation, exclusion, broken relationships or lonely abandonment. Estranged specifically suggests a relationship that has become distant.
These can make a scene unsettling: strange and uncanny, threatening future trouble, unwelcoming, or disturbingly distorted.
These describe giving freely, wishing others well, responding to suffering, showing fondness or offering gentle care. Their meanings overlap without being identical.
These direct a written response: compare ideas, examine methods, clarify reasons, investigate possibilities, discuss evidence, make judgements, interpret meanings or describe details.
These describe acquiring, possessing, overvaluing or refusing to share wealth. Grasping can mean greedy as well as physically reaching. Frugal means economical and need not imply greed.
These concern sorrow about past actions. Contrite, remorseful and penitent describe people; penitence and regret name feelings or states, with repentance also involving a wish to put things right.

group: Words for a lack of care
explanation: These express insensitivity, lack of concern, disregard or failure to provide attention and care. They help explain Scrooge’s early treatment of other people.
Repetition reuses language, an echo recalls something earlier, a motif is a recurring detail or idea, and alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds.
An allegory uses a story to embody wider ideas. Symbolism and the verb symbolise concern representation, while metaphor describes one thing as another.
These describe depicting, standing for, clarifying by example, making visible, mirroring or conveying an idea through a symbol. Symbolise also belongs to the group about representation.
Reinforce strengthens a claim. Undermine weakens it, challenge questions it, and criticise identifies faults. All four describe how an argument can be treated.
The complete terms are direct address, semantic field, cyclical structure, pathetic fallacy and extended metaphor.
Marley warns Scrooge before the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Christmas Present and Christmas Yet to Come visit him. Future is the short label for the last spirit.
These are family names. Ebenezer, Jacob, Bob and Dick are given names belonging to characters with these surnames.
Scrooge mentions these to the charity collectors in Stave One. He uses the existing institutions and system as a reason to refuse a donation.
These are vehicles associated with the novella’s world. A hearse carries a coffin; the image of one appears when Scrooge enters his dark home.
These name rooms or spaces inside a home. Such vocabulary helps distinguish the domestic settings around Scrooge, Fred and the Cratchits.
These are pieces of furniture. A bureau is a desk or cabinet with drawers, rather than a room in a house.
These hold money. The group concerns containers, rather than coins or the documents used to record business.
These name coins from the older British currency system. They provide useful vocabulary for the novella’s references to money.
These describe family relationships. Scrooge is Fred’s uncle; Fan is Scrooge’s sister; Bob is Tiny Tim’s father.
These are fittings or objects used to close, lock or secure a door. Scrooge’s concern with shutting himself away makes this a useful group.
These are records, agreements or requests for payment associated with business. A ledger records accounts; a deed records a legal agreement or ownership.
In Stave Five, Scrooge compares himself to these when describing how light, happy, merry and giddy he feels.
These describe ways of offering money, time, assistance or company. Scrooge’s change becomes visible through actions of this kind.
These name emotions. Following changes in Scrooge’s feelings helps explain his response to the spirits’ visits.
These are parts of the body. Dickens also uses bodily images, including the heart and hand, to suggest attitudes towards other people.
These describe weather or atmospheric conditions. Cold and obscured visibility are especially important in the novella’s opening setting.
Fred uses these four adjectives together when defending Christmas in Stave One. They emphasise goodwill, generosity and enjoyment.
These suggest light being emitted or reflected. Dickens repeatedly uses brightness to describe warmth, pleasure and the spirits’ appearances.
These divide, enclose or separate. They offer useful ways of thinking about Scrooge’s isolation and the protective outer shell suggested by the oyster image.
These verbs describe using the senses. Sensory detail helps make the novella’s streets, meals and supernatural encounters vivid.
These concern receiving or visiting people. Fred’s repeated invitation contrasts with Scrooge’s early refusal to welcome company.
Used as verbs, these concern working out amounts or checking figures. They connect with the counting-house and Scrooge’s habit of measuring value through money.
These concern making, finishing or repairing fabric. The novella’s domestic work and the Cratchits’ limited clothing make this vocabulary useful.
These can describe sounds made by metal objects or bells. Chains, cash and striking clocks contribute to the novella’s soundscape.
These name laughter or enjoyment. Mirth means amusement, while a guffaw is a loud laugh. Shared laughter is prominent at Fred’s party.
These nouns concern compassion towards someone who could be blamed or punished. They help describe the possibility of another chance for Scrooge.
These concern money or assets, though their meanings differ: profit is what remains after costs, revenue is money received, and capital is wealth available for use or investment.
The suffix -less commonly means without. These adjectives describe the absence of shelter, friends, help, hope, money, love or power.
The Ghost of Christmas Present takes Scrooge to this gathering. The plump sister is one of Fred’s wife’s sisters, whom Topper pursues during blindman’s buff.

group: Fruit in the Stave Three shops
explanation: Dickens includes these fresh or dried fruits in the abundant shops on Christmas morning. Their variety helps convey plenty and sensory pleasure.
These adjectives appear together when the two children emerge from the spirit’s robe. They make social neglect visible through disturbing physical detail.
These can describe limited strength or poor health. Delicate has other meanings too; here it means physically vulnerable.
Scrooge recalls these fictional figures while revisiting his lonely schooldays in Stave Two. His books supplied imagined companions.
These nouns concern wealth, comfort or ample supplies. They can describe material plenty without necessarily implying the selfishness conveyed by avarice.
These concern deprivation or insufficient resources. Destitution and penury suggest extreme poverty; scarcity means a shortage, which need not involve money.
These auxiliaries express meanings such as possibility, ability, obligation and prediction. Distinguishing possibility from certainty is especially useful when analysing Scrooge’s future.
These link contrasting ideas, though their grammar differs. They can introduce a qualification, an opposing view or a difference between characters and scenes.
These add a point or show agreement and similarity. They are useful when connecting evidence, but similarly and likewise specifically require a meaningful parallel.
These can connect a reason to its consequence or conclusion. A result link should follow reasoning that actually supports the next point.

These describe narrative person or access to knowledge. An omniscient narrator can know more than one character; limited narration restricts what is available. They are analytical options, not four labels all applicable to this novella.

These concern a narrative’s relationship with past and future events. Analepsis is a backward shift and prolepsis a forward one; foreshadowing hints at what is to come without necessarily moving the action forwards.
These verbs describe drawing conclusions or proposing explanations. Inference and deduction depend on reasoning; conjecture and speculation make the uncertainty of a suggestion more explicit.

These offer different ways of classifying stories. Gothic fiction often uses fear and the supernatural; allegories embody wider ideas, while fables and parables convey lessons. The terms have distinct meanings.
These concern the preparation, transport or burial of the dead and places associated with burial. Such vocabulary becomes especially significant during the last spirit’s visit.

group: Capitalised abstract ideas in the novella
explanation: Dickens gives these abstract ideas conspicuous capitals. Ignorance and Want are named as children; Belle identifies Gain as Scrooge’s master-passion. The charity collector invokes Abundance, and the second spirit’s torch resembles Plenty’s horn.
These nouns can name physical weakness or vulnerability. They provide more precise alternatives to simply describing someone as weak, although fragility can also apply to objects or situations.

These concern things changing or failing to last. Mutability stresses the capacity for change; transience and ephemerality stress short duration. They can help distinguish the novella’s treatment of reform from its treatment of passing time.

group: Reducing people and relationships to things
explanation: These name related reductions of human identity or value. Objectification treats a person as an object; commodification treats something as a tradeable commodity; reification treats an abstraction or relationship as a thing. Scrooge’s financial view of people offers a starting point for these interpretations.
